bibliography.note: Journal of Fish Biology 33(4): 623–636 (1988), Wright R. M. & Shoesmith E. A. Matches.

claims.claim: in an English gravel pit pike eggs hatched better on sand and silt (11 %) than on plants (2.5 %) in 1986
claims.note: Full text not obtained. The GWCT abstract gives egg-survival experiments with overall hatching success of 11 % on sand/silt against 2.5 % on aquatic plants (1986), and 18.9 % on undisturbed against 7.9 % on disturbed sand/silt (1987), in Main Lake, a gravel pit in Buckinghamshire.

claims.claim: even though age-0 survival was higher in a densely vegetated lake (Wright & Shoesmith 1988; abstract)
claims.note: Full text not obtained, and the abstract the paper cites does NOT say this: it covers fecundity, egg size, egg density, stage-1-to-fry survival (3–6 %), egg loss (9–10 % per day) and the hatching experiments. The age-0 comparison is in the abstract of Wright 1990 (J. Fish Biol. 36: 215–229, GWCT record wright1990a): 0-group survival to November 1987 was 0.00315 % of potential eggs in St Peter's Lake against 0.00175 % in Main Lake, recruitment differing mainly with the abundance of aquatic vegetation. The rewrite should cite Wright 1990 (abstract) for this part.

claims.claim: hatching in an English gravel pit was 11 % on sand and silt against 2.5 % on plants (Wright & Shoesmith 1988, abstract)
claims.note: As the first claim: the abstract gives these numbers (1986 experiment); the full text, needed for the design (how eggs were placed, n, which plants), was not obtained.
